claims.claim: Calcium transients elicited by five action potentials at 25 Hz were significantly smaller in Grin1-cKO animals (0.025 ± 0.004 ΔG/R) compared to control (0.046 ± 0.01 ΔG/R).
claims.source: We found that Ca2+ transients (CaTs) elicited by direct current injection in the GC soma (five action potentials, 25 Hz) were significantly smaller in Grin1-cKO animals as compared to control (Figure 5C–E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by two-photon calcium imaging shown in Figure 5C-E with statistical significance (U = 0.017).

claims.claim: D-APV (100 µM) significantly reduced the fifth peak of calcium transients from 0.155 ± 0.04 to 0.138 ± 0.03 ΔG/R.
claims.source: D-APV (100 µM) significantly reduced the fifth peak (P5) of CaTs (baseline 0.155 ± 0.04, D-APV 0.138 ± 0.03, n = 13 boutons, three line scans per bouton, 10 animals; baseline vs D-APV, p=0.00642, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by two-photon calcium imaging under physiological Mg2+ concentration shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: The fifth peak of calcium transients is stable in naïve conditions (baseline 0.104 ± 0.026, naïve 0.105 ± 0.026).
claims.source: In naïve conditions P5 of CaTs is stable (baseline 0.104 ± 0.026, naïve 0.105 ± 0.026, n = 12 boutons, three line scans per bouton, 10 animals; baseline vs naïve, p=0.255, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by control calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: The first peak of calcium transients is not affected by D-APV (baseline 0.05 ± 0.017; D-APV 0.047 ± 0.014).
claims.source: The first peak (P1) of CaTs is not affected by D-APV (baseline 0.05 ± 0.017; D-APV 0.047 ± 0.014; baseline vs D-APV, p=0.485, Wilcoxon signed-rank test) and is stable in naïve conditions (baseline 0.033 ± 0.009; naïve 0.032 ± 0.009, baseline vs naïve, p=0.196, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Glutamate two-photon uncaging-induced calcium transients in dendritic spine heads of GCs were strongly reduced in Grin1-cKO animals (0.004 ± 0.003 ΔG/R) compared to controls (0.053 ± 0.01 ΔG/R).
claims.source: We first confirmed that glutamate 2PU-induced CaTs in dendritic spine heads of GCs were strongly reduced in Grin1-cKO animals as compared to controls (Figure 6B,C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by two-photon glutamate uncaging experiments shown in Figure 6B-C with statistical significance (p=0.00088).

claims.claim: Grin1-cKO animals exhibited reduced ΔG/R signals compared to control regardless of laser power intensity.
claims.source: To verify that reduced Ca2+ signals (ΔG/R) were a result of Grin1 deletion and not differences in uncaging laser power, we performed a laser power intensity–response curve and found that Grin1-cKO animals exhibited reduced ΔG/R signals as compared to control regardless of laser power intensity (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by laser power intensity-response curve analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Single glutamate uncaging pulses were insufficient to drive detectable calcium transients in control mf boutons.
claims.source: We next measured glutamate 2PU-induced CaTs in mf giant boutons (identified as in Figure 5B) and found that single uncaging pulses were insufficient to drive detectable CaTs in control boutons (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by two-photon glutamate uncaging experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: A burst of two-photon glutamate uncaging stimulation (5 pulses, 25 Hz) induced calcium transients in mf boutons of control (0.014 ± 0.005 ΔG/R) but not in Grin1-cKO animals (−0.00012 ± −0.0006 ΔG/R).
claims.source: However, a burst of 2PU stimulation (5 pulses, 25 Hz) induced CaTs in mf boutons of control but not in Grin1-cKO animals (Figure 6D,E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by two-photon glutamate uncaging experiments shown in Figure 6D-E with statistical significance (p=0.015).

claims.claim: Calcium transients elicited by two-photon glutamate uncaging were abolished by D-APV application.
claims.source: Additionally, CaTs elicited by 2PU stimulation were abolished by D-APV application (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by two-photon glutamate uncaging experiments with D-APV shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Control animals display robust ΔG/R signals compared to Grin1-cKO animals at varying laser power intensities.
claims.source: Control animals display robust ΔG/R signals as compared to Grin1-cKO animals at varying laser power intensities (six spines, three line scans per spine, six animals per group, U = 0.00507 per power intensity, Mann–Whitney test).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by laser power intensity analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Repetitive pulses (5 pulses) result in larger ΔG/R signals compared to single pulses in mf boutons.
claims.source: Repetitive pulses result in larger ΔG/R signals as compared to single pulses (n = 6 boutons, three line scans per bouton, six animals, p=0.03603, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of single vs. multiple pulse uncaging shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: D-APV application (100 µM) blocks calcium transients elicited by glutamate uncaging in mf boutons (baseline 0.0103 ± 0.0016, D-APV −0.004 ± 0.0024).
claims.source: Summary data of D-APV block on glutamate uncaging elicited CaTs (baseline 0.0103 ± 0.0016, D-APV −0.004 ± 0.0024, n = 4 boutons, three line scans per bouton, three animals; U = 0.0304, Mann–Whitney test, baseline vs D-APV).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by two-photon glutamate uncaging experiments with D-APV shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3C.

claims.claim: GluN1-deficient mf boutons showed approximately 50% impairment in BDNF release compared to control during repetitive stimulation.
claims.source: We found that GluN1-deficient mf boutons showed a significant (~50%) impairment in BDNF release as compared to control (Figure 7C–D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by BDNF-pHluorin imaging experiments shown in Figure 7C-D.

claims.claim: BDNF-pHluorin signal during the last 100 s reveals larger BDNF release in control animals (−18% ± 3%) compared to Grin1-cKO (−8 ± 1%) during repetitive stimulation.
claims.source: Quantification of BDNF-pHluorin signal in (C) during the last 100 s reveals larger BDNF release in control animals as compared to Grin1-cKO (control −18% ± 3%, n = 9 slices, five animals; Grin1-cKO −8 ± 1%, n = 10 slices, five animals; Grin1-cKO vs control, p=0.00648, unpaired t-test).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by BDNF-pHluorin imaging analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: GluN1-lacking mf boutons displayed altered BDNF release compared to control during burst stimulation (5 pulses, 100 Hz, ×50).
claims.source: Furthermore, using a more physiological pattern of burst stimulation, GluN1-lacking mf boutons still displayed altered BDNF release as compared to control (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by BDNF-pHluorin imaging with burst stimulation shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: BDNF-pHluorin signal during the last 100 s reveals larger BDNF release in control animals (−8.9% ± 2%) compared to Grin1-cKO (−3.5 ± 1%) during burst stimulation.
claims.source: Quantification of BDNF-pHluorin signal in (B) during the last 100 s reveals larger BDNF release in control animals as compared to Grin1-cKO (control −8.9% ± 2%, n = 7 slices, five animals; Grin1-cKO −3.5 ± 1%, n = 11 slices, five animals; Grin1-cKO vs control, p=0.0305, unpaired t-test).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by BDNF-pHluorin imaging analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Bath application of MK-801 (50 µM) had no significant effect on burst-induced depression or facilitation at mf-CA3 interneuron synapses.
claims.source: We found that MK-801 bath application had no effect on burst-induced facilitation or depression (Figure 8B), suggesting preNMDARs do not play a role at mf-IN synapses in CA3.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings from CA3 interneurons shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: Bath application of MK-801 (50 µM) reduced low-frequency facilitation at mf-mossy cell synapses from 339 ± 41% to 258 ± 29%.
claims.source: Similar to mf-CA3 synapses, we found that MK-801 reduced LFF (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings from mossy cells shown in Figure 8C with statistical significance (p=0.00152).

claims.claim: CA3 interneuron burst-induced facilitation of mf transmission was stable (baseline 273 ± 30%, naïve 294 ± 33%).
claims.source: Stable CA3 IN burst-induced facilitation of mf-CA3 transmission (baseline 273 ± 30%, naïve 294 ± 33%, n = 10 cells, six animals; p=0.298, paired t-test, baseline vs naïve).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by control experiments shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Low-frequency facilitation of AMPAR-EPSCs in hilar mossy cells was stable (baseline 288 ± 51%, naïve 291 ± 29%).
claims.source: Stable low-frequency facilitation (LFF) of AMPAR-EPSCs in hilar MCs (baseline 288 ± 51%, naïve 291 ± 29%, n = 7 cells, six animals; p=0.937, paired t-test, baseline vs naïve).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by control experiments shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors at mossy fiber boutons can be activated by physiologically relevant patterns of activity.
claims.source: Here, we report that presynaptic NMDA receptors (preNMDARs) at mossy fiber boutons in the rodent hippocampus can be activated by physiologically relevant patterns of activity and selectively enhance short-term synaptic plasticity at mossy fiber inputs onto CA3 pyramidal cells and mossy cells, but not onto inhibitory interneurons.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by multiple experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors selectively enhance short-term synaptic plasticity at mossy fiber inputs onto CA3 pyramidal cells and mossy cells, but not onto inhibitory interneurons.
claims.source: Here, we report that presynaptic NMDA receptors (preNMDARs) at mossy fiber boutons in the rodent hippocampus can be activated by physiologically relevant patterns of activity and selectively enhance short-term synaptic plasticity at mossy fiber inputs onto CA3 pyramidal cells and mossy cells, but not onto inhibitory interneurons.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 1-4 and Figure 8.

claims.claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors facilitate brain-derived neurotrophic factor release at mossy fiber synapses.
claims.source: Moreover, preNMDARs facilitate brain-derived neurotrophic factor release and contribute to presynaptic calcium rise.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by BDNF-pHluorin imaging data in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors contribute to presynaptic calcium rise at mossy fiber boutons.
claims.source: Moreover, preNMDARs facilitate brain-derived neurotrophic factor release and contribute to presynaptic calcium rise.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by two-photon calcium imaging data in Figures 5 and 6.

claims.claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors fine-tune mossy fiber neurotransmission by increasing presynaptic calcium.
claims.source: Taken together, our results indicate that by increasing presynaptic calcium, preNMDARs fine-tune mossy fiber neurotransmission and can control information transfer during dentate granule cell burst activity that normally occur in vivo.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by calcium imaging and electrophysiology data throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors can control information transfer during dentate granule cell burst activity that normally occur in vivo.
claims.source: Taken together, our results indicate that by increasing presynaptic calcium, preNMDARs fine-tune mossy fiber neurotransmission and can control information transfer during dentate granule cell burst activity that normally occur in vivo.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by burst stimulation experiments in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Anatomical evidence for presynaptic NMDA receptors arose from an immunoelectron microscopy study revealing NMDARs at the mossy fiber giant bouton of the monkey hippocampus.
claims.source: Anatomical evidence for preNMDARs arose from an immunoelectron microscopy study revealing NMDARs at the mossy fiber giant bouton of the monkey hippocampus (Siegel et al., 1994), followed by functional studies in the entorhinal cortex, indicating that preNMDARs tonically increase spontaneous glutamate release and also facilitate evoked release in a frequency-dependent manner (Berretta and Jones, 1996; Woodhall et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Siegel et al., 1994).

claims.claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors tonically increase spontaneous glutamate release in the entorhinal cortex.
claims.source: Anatomical evidence for preNMDARs arose from an immunoelectron microscopy study revealing NMDARs at the mossy fiber giant bouton of the monkey hippocampus (Siegel et al., 1994), followed by functional studies in the entorhinal cortex, indicating that preNMDARs tonically increase spontaneous glutamate release and also facilitate evoked release in a frequency-dependent manner (Berretta and Jones, 1996; Woodhall et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Berretta and Jones, 1996; Woodhall et al., 2001).

claims.claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors facilitate evoked release in a frequency-dependent manner in the entorhinal cortex.
claims.source: Anatomical evidence for preNMDARs arose from an immunoelectron microscopy study revealing NMDARs at the mossy fiber giant bouton of the monkey hippocampus (Siegel et al., 1994), followed by functional studies in the entorhinal cortex, indicating that preNMDARs tonically increase spontaneous glutamate release and also facilitate evoked release in a frequency-dependent manner (Berretta and Jones, 1996; Woodhall et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Berretta and Jones, 1996; Woodhall et al., 2001).

claims.claim: The mossy fiber-CA3 synapse displays uniquely robust frequency facilitation both in vitro and in vivo.
claims.source: This synapse displays uniquely robust frequency facilitation both in vitro (Nicoll and Schmitz, 2005; Salin et al., 1996; Vyleta et al., 2016) and in vivo (Hagena and Manahan-Vaughan, 2010; Vandael et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The molecular basis of short-term plasticity at mossy fiber synapses is not fully understood but likely relies on diverse presynaptic mechanisms that increase glutamate release.
claims.source: The molecular basis of this short-term plasticity is not fully understood but likely relies on diverse presynaptic mechanisms that increase glutamate release (Jackman and Regehr, 2017; Rebola et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Jackman and Regehr, 2017; Rebola et al., 2017).

claims.claim: Short-term, use-dependent facilitation is believed to play a critical role in information transfer, circuit dynamics, and short-term memory.
claims.source: Short-term, use-dependent facilitation is believed to play a critical role in information transfer, circuit dynamics, and short-term memory (Abbott and Regehr, 2004; Jackman and Regehr, 2017; Klug et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Abbott and Regehr, 2004; Jackman and Regehr, 2017; Klug et al., 2012).

claims.claim: The mf-CA3 synapse can strongly drive the CA3 network during short bursts of presynaptic activity.
claims.source: The mf-CA3 synapse can strongly drive the CA3 network during short bursts of presynaptic activity (Chamberland et al., 2018; Henze et al., 2002; Vyleta et al., 2016; Zucca et al., 2017), an effect that likely results from two key properties of this synapse, namely, its strong frequency facilitation and proximal dendritic localization.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Chamberland et al., 2018; Henze et al., 2002; Vyleta et al., 2016; Zucca et al., 2017).

claims.claim: Mossy fibers contain one of the highest expression levels of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF).
claims.source: Intriguingly, mfs contain one of the highest expression levels of brain-derived neurotrophic factor, BDNF (Conner et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Conner et al., 1997).

claims.claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors were implicated in BDNF release at corticostriatal synapses.
claims.source: While preNMDARs were implicated in BDNF release at corticostriatal synapses (Park et al., 2014), whether putative preNMDARs impact BDNF release at mf synapses remains unexplored.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Park et al., 2014).

claims.claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors at mossy fibers may facilitate information transfer and provide an important point of regulation in the DG-CA3 circuit by modulating both glutamate and BDNF release.
claims.source: Thus, preNMDARs at mfs may facilitate information transfer and provide an important point of regulation in the DG-CA3 circuit by modulating both glutamate and BDNF release.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Introduction and supported by experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors are adjacent to the release sites at mf-CA3 synapses.
claims.source: In contrast, at mf-CA3 synapses, we found that preNMDARs are adjacent to the release sites, suggesting a direct control on glutamate release from mf boutons.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the electron microscopy data showing presynaptic localization of GluN1 near active zones.

claims.claim: The reduction in facilitation of AMPAR transmission by NMDAR antagonism could be due to dampening of CA3 recurrent activity.
claims.source: The reduction in facilitation of AMPAR transmission could be due to dampening of CA3 recurrent activity by NMDAR antagonism (Henze et al., 2000; Kwon and Castillo, 2008; Nicoll and Schmitz, 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a potential alternative explanation and is addressed by subsequent experiments.

claims.claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors facilitate neurotransmitter release in a target cell-specific manner.
claims.source: We also found that preNMDARs facilitate neurotransmitter release in a target cell-specific manner.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by data in Figure 8 showing differential effects on excitatory vs. inhibitory neurons.

claims.claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptor facilitation of mf synapses onto glutamatergic neurons but not GABAergic interneurons may fine-tune the CA3 circuit by increasing the excitatory/inhibitory balance.
claims.source: Thus, preNMDAR facilitation of mf synapses onto glutamatergic neurons but not GABAergic INs (Figure 8) may fine-tune the CA3 circuit by increasing the excitatory/inhibitory balance.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by data in Figure 8.

claims.claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors may provide an important site of neuromodulatory control given the multiple signaling cascades known to regulate NMDARs.
claims.source: Given the multiple signaling cascades known to regulate NMDARs (Lau and Zukin, 2007; Sanz-Clemente et al., 2013), preNMDARs at mf synapses may provide an important site of neuromodulatory control.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations to previous work on NMDAR regulation.

claims.claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors could play a role in vivo during subtle presynaptic activities.
claims.source: While most evidence, at least using robust induction protocols in vitro, indicates that long-term forms of presynaptic plasticity at mf synapses can occur in the absence of NMDAR activation (Castillo, 2012; Nicoll and Schmitz, 2005), our findings do not discard the possibility that preNMDARs could play a role in vivo during subtle presynaptic activities.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion as a speculative possibility.

claims.claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors could regulate long-term synaptic plasticity by controlling BDNF release.
claims.source: As previously reported for corticostriatal LTP (Park et al., 2014), preNMDARs could regulate long-term synaptic plasticity by controlling BDNF release, which is consistent with BDNF-TrkB signaling being implicated in mf-CA3 LTP (Schildt et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: BDNF could facilitate glutamate release by enhancing NMDAR function at the presynapse.
claims.source: In addition, BDNF could facilitate glutamate release by enhancing NMDAR function at the presynapse, as previously suggested (Chen et al., 2014; Madara and Levine, 2008), although the precise mechanism(s) remain unclear.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: By potentiating mf-CA3 transmission, BDNF could also promote epileptic activity.
claims.source: By potentiating mf-CA3 transmission, BDNF could also promote epileptic activity (McNamara and Scharfman, 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Dysregulation of NMDARs is commonly implicated in the pathophysiology of brain disorders such as schizophrenia, autism, and epilepsy.
claims.source: Lastly, dysregulation of NMDARs is commonly implicated in the pathophysiology of brain disorders such as schizophrenia, autism, and epilepsy (Lau and Zukin, 2007; Paoletti et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Lau and Zukin, 2007; Paoletti et al., 2013).

claims.claim: Presynaptic NMDAR expression and function have been suggested to be altered in experimental models of disease, including neuropathic pain and epilepsy.
claims.source: PreNMDAR expression and function have been suggested to be altered in experimental models of disease, including neuropathic pain (Chen et al., 2019; Zeng et al., 2006) and epilepsy (Yang et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Chen et al., 2019; Zeng et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2006).

claims.claim: The development of specific presynaptic NMDAR tools is required to determine the functional impact of these receptors in vivo.
claims.source: The development of specific preNMDAR tools is required to determine the functional impact of these receptors in vivo.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion as a future direction.

claims.claim: Dentate granule cells in vivo typically fire in brief bursts.
claims.source: GCs in vivo typically fire in brief bursts (Diamantaki et al., 2016; GoodSmith et al., 2017; Henze et al., 2002; Pernía-Andrade and Jonas, 2014; Senzai and Buzsáki, 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work on in vivo GC firing patterns.

claims.claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors contribute to synaptic facilitation that occurs during physiologically relevant patterns of activity.
claims.source: To test whether preNMDARs contribute to synaptic facilitation that occurs during more physiological patterns of activity, mfs were activated with brief bursts (five stimuli, 25 Hz).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by burst stimulation experiments in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors, by facilitating glutamate release during bursting activity, could bring CA3 pyramidal neurons to threshold and trigger postsynaptic action potentials.
claims.source: Lastly, we tested whether preNMDARs, by facilitating glutamate release during bursting activity, could bring CA3 pyramidal neurons to threshold and trigger postsynaptic action potentials.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by action potential recordings in Figure 4F-G.

claims.claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors at mf-CA3 synapses can contribute to information transfer from the DG to CA3.
claims.source: Altogether, these results indicate that preNMDARs at mf-CA3 synapses can contribute to information transfer from the DG to CA3.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors could facilitate glutamate and BDNF release by increasing presynaptic Ca2+ rise.
claims.source: PreNMDARs could facilitate glutamate and BDNF release by increasing presynaptic Ca2+ rise (Bouvier et al., 2016; Buchanan et al., 2012; Corlew et al., 2008; Park et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work and tested experimentally in Figures 5-7.

claims.claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors contribute significantly to presynaptic Ca2+ rise in mf boutons.
claims.source: Thus, preNMDARs contribute significantly to presynaptic Ca2+ rise in mf boutons, and by this means likely facilitates synaptic transmission, although a potential contribution of Ca2+ rise-independent effects cannot be discarded.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by calcium imaging data in Figures 5 and 6.

claims.claim: Brief bursts of glutamate two-photon uncaging, mimicking endogenous release during physiological patterns of activity, induces presynaptic Ca2+ influx in mf boutons by activating presynaptic NMDA receptors.
claims.source: These findings indicate that brief bursts of glutamate 2PU, a manipulation that mimics endogenous release of glutamate during physiological patterns of activity, induces presynaptic Ca2+ influx in mf boutons by activating preNMDARs.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by two-photon glutamate uncaging data in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors contribute significantly to BDNF release during repetitive or burst stimulation of mf synapses.
claims.source: Taken together, our results suggest preNMDARs contribute significantly to BDNF release during repetitive or burst stimulation of mf synapses.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by BDNF-pHluorin imaging data in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors enhance mf short-term plasticity in a target cell-specific manner.
claims.source: Specifically, our results show that preNMDARs enhance mf short-term plasticity in a target cell-specific manner.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by data in Figures 1-4 and Figure 8.

claims.claim: By enhancing glutamate release onto excitatory neurons but not inhibitory interneurons, presynaptic NMDA receptors increase GC-CA3 spike transfer.
claims.source: By enhancing glutamate release onto excitatory neurons but not inhibitory INs, preNMDARs increase GC-CA3 spike transfer.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by data in Figures 4 and 8.

claims.claim: Upon repetitive activity, presynaptic NMDA receptors promote BDNF release from mf boutons.
claims.source: Lastly, upon repetitive activity, preNMDARs promote BDNF release from mf boutons.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by BDNF-pHluorin imaging data in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors act as autoreceptors to boost both glutamate and BDNF release at mf synapses.
claims.source: Taken together, our findings indicate that preNMDARs act as autoreceptors to boost both glutamate and BDNF release at mf synapses.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: By regulating information flow in the DG-CA3 circuit, presynaptic NMDA receptors may play a significant role in learning and memory.
claims.source: By regulating information flow in the DG-CA3 circuit, preNMDARs may play a significant role in learning and memory.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion as a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claims.claim: Immunogold electron microscopy is a more precise localization method than immunoperoxidase electron microscopy.
claims.source: Subsequent studies that used immunogold electron microscopy, a more precise localization method, identified NMDARs on the presynaptic membrane in a number of brain structures, including neocortex (Fujisawa and Aoki, 2003; Larsen et al., 2011), hippocampus (Berg et al., 2013; Jourdain et al., 2007; McGuinness et al., 2010), and amygdala (Pickel et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors are well positioned to modulate neurotransmitter release because they are close to the active zone.
claims.source: Moreover, we found that these receptors are close to the active zone and therefore well positioned to modulate neurotransmitter release.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by electron microscopy data in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Somatodendritic potentials generated by NMDARs could signal to nerve terminals and lead to presynaptic Ca2+ elevations in the cerebellum and neocortex.
claims.source: Previous work in the cerebellum and neocortex suggested that somatodendritic potentials generated by NMDARs could signal to nerve terminals and lead to presynaptic Ca2+ elevations (Christie and Jahr, 2008; Christie and Jahr, 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Christie and Jahr, 2008; Christie and Jahr, 2009).

claims.claim: Changes in neurotransmitter release resulting from NMDAR antagonism could be due to somatodendritic NMDARs but not necessarily presynaptic NMDARs residing on nerve terminals.
claims.source: Thus, changes in neurotransmitter release resulting from NMDAR antagonism could be due to somatodendritic NMDARs but not necessarily preNMDARs residing on nerve terminals (Duguid, 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation to previous work (Duguid, 2013).

claims.claim: It is extremely unlikely that somatodendritic NMDARs could explain the reduction of short-term plasticity at mf synapses by NMDAR antagonism.
claims.source: However, we showed that focal NMDAR antagonism far from the somatodendritic compartment and in transected axons still reduced short-term plasticity at mf synapses (Figure 3), making it extremely unlikely that somatodendritic NMDARs could explain our results.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by experiments in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors can operate as coincidence detectors at some synapses.
claims.source: There is evidence that preNMDARs can operate as coincidence detectors at some synapses (Duguid, 2013; Wong et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Duguid, 2013; Wong et al., 2021).

claims.claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors contribute to low-frequency facilitation at the mf-CA3 synapse.
claims.source: At the mf-CA3 synapse, we found that preNMDARs contribute to LFF (i.e. 1 s inter-stimulus interval).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by data in Figures 1-3.

claims.claim: Coincidence detection may not be an essential requirement for mf presynaptic NMDA receptors to modulate glutamate release.
claims.source: However, coincidence detection may not be an essential requirement for mf preNMDARs to modulate glutamate release.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claims.claim: At resting membrane potential, the NMDAR conductance is not zero and the driving force for Ca2+ influx is high.
claims.source: Of note, at resting membrane potential, the NMDAR conductance is not zero and the driving force for Ca2+ influx is high (Paoletti et al., 2013; Traynelis et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Paoletti et al., 2013; Traynelis et al., 2010).

claims.claim: Mf presynaptic NMDA receptors may exhibit low-voltage dependence.
claims.source: It is also conceivable that mf preNMDARs exhibit low-voltage dependence, as it has been reported at other synapses (Wong et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion as a speculative possibility supported by citation to previous work (Wong et al., 2021).

claims.claim: The somatodendritic compartment of GCs can generate sub-threshold depolarizations at mf terminals (excitatory presynaptic potentials).
claims.source: Remarkably, the somatodendritic compartment of GCs can generate sub-threshold depolarizations at mf terminals (a.k.a. excitatory presynaptic potentials) (Alle and Geiger, 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Alle and Geiger, 2006).

claims.claim: Excitatory presynaptic potentials might reduce the need for coincidence detection and transiently boost the functional impact of mf presynaptic NMDA receptors by alleviating the magnesium blockade.
claims.source: By alleviating the magnesium blockade, these potentials might reduce the need for coincidence detection and transiently boost the functional impact of mf preNMDARs.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion as a speculative mechanism.

claims.claim: The presence of presynaptic NMDA receptors is downregulated during development in neocortex and hippocampus.
claims.source: While the presence of preNMDARs is downregulated during development both in neocortex (Corlew et al., 2007; Larsen et al., 2011) and in hippocampus (Mameli et al., 2005), we were able to detect functional preNMDARs in young adult rats (P17–P28) and mice (P30–P44), once mf connections are fully developed (Amaral and Dent, 1981).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Corlew et al., 2007; Larsen et al., 2011; Mameli et al., 2005).

claims.claim: Functional presynaptic NMDA receptors were detected in young adult rats (P17-P28) and mice (P30-P44), once mf connections are fully developed.
claims.source: While the presence of preNMDARs is downregulated during development both in neocortex (Corlew et al., 2007; Larsen et al., 2011) and in hippocampus (Mameli et al., 2005), we were able to detect functional preNMDARs in young adult rats (P17–P28) and mice (P30–P44), once mf connections are fully developed (Amaral and Dent, 1981).

claims.source: Functional preNMDARs have been identified in axonal growth cones of hippocampal and neocortical neurons, suggesting that these receptors are important for regulating early synapse formation (Gill et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Gill et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2011).

claims.claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors could play an important role at immature mf synapses and functional integration of new born GCs into the mature hippocampus.
claims.source: Because GCs undergo adult neurogenesis, and adult-born GCs establish new connections in the mature brain, preNMDARs could also play an important role at immature mf synapses and functional integration of new born GCs into the mature hippocampus (Toni and Schinder, 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion as a speculative possibility supported by citation to previous work (Toni and Schinder, 2015).

claims.source: Moreover, experience can modulate the expression and composition of preNMDARs in neocortex (Larsen et al., 2014), a possibility not investigated in our study.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Larsen et al., 2014).

claims.claim: The glutamate that activates presynaptic NMDA receptors may originate from the presynaptic terminal, the postsynaptic cell, nearby synapses or neighboring glial cells.
claims.source: The glutamate that activates preNMDARs may originate from the presynaptic terminal, the postsynaptic cell, nearby synapses or neighboring glial cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion as a general consideration.

claims.claim: Activation of presynaptic NMDA receptors at mf synapses requires activity-dependent release of glutamate that likely arises from mf boutons.
claims.source: Our results indicate that activation of preNMDARs at mf synapses requires activity-dependent release of glutamate that likely arises from mf boutons, although other sources cannot be discarded, including astrocytes.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by experimental findings.

claims.claim: At medial entorhinal inputs to GCs, presynaptic NMDA receptors appear to be localized away from the presynaptic release sites and facing astrocytes, consistent with preNMDAR activation by gliotransmitters.
claims.source: For instance, at medial entorhinal inputs to GCs, preNMDARs appear to be localized away from the presynaptic release sites and facing astrocytes, consistent with preNMDAR activation by gliotransmitters (Jourdain et al., 2007; Savtchouk et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Jourdain et al., 2007; Savtchouk et al., 2019).

claims.claim: The precise mechanism by which presynaptic NMDA receptors facilitate neurotransmitter release is poorly understood.
claims.source: The precise mechanism by which preNMDARs facilitate neurotransmitter release is poorly understood, but it may include Ca2+ influx through the receptor and depolarization of the presynaptic terminal with subsequent activation of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (Banerjee et al., 2016; Corlew et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The mechanism by which presynaptic NMDA receptors facilitate neurotransmitter release may include Ca2+ influx through the receptor and depolarization of the presynaptic terminal with subsequent activation of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels.
claims.source: The precise mechanism by which preNMDARs facilitate neurotransmitter release is poorly understood, but it may include Ca2+ influx through the receptor and depolarization of the presynaptic terminal with subsequent activation of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (Banerjee et al., 2016; Corlew et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Banerjee et al., 2016; Corlew et al., 2008).

claims.claim: NMDA receptors have high Ca2+ permeability.
claims.source: In support of this mechanism is the high Ca2+ permeability of NMDARs (Paoletti et al., 2013; Rogers and Dani, 1995).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Paoletti et al., 2013; Rogers and Dani, 1995).

claims.claim: Presynaptic sub-threshold depolarization and subsequent activation of presynaptic voltage-gated Ca2+ channels is a common mechanism by which presynaptic ionotropic receptors facilitate neurotransmitter release.
claims.source: Besides, presynaptic sub-threshold depolarization and subsequent activation of presynaptic voltage-gated Ca2+ channels is a common mechanism by which presynaptic ionotropic receptors facilitate neurotransmitter release (Engelman and MacDermott, 2004; Pinheiro and Mulle, 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Engelman and MacDermott, 2004; Pinheiro and Mulle, 2008).

claims.claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors may act in a metabotropic manner.
claims.source: PreNMDARs may also act in a metabotropic manner (Dore et al., 2016) and facilitate spontaneous transmitter release independent of Ca2+ influx (Abrahamsson et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Dore et al., 2016; Abrahamsson et al., 2017).

claims.source: PreNMDARs may also act in a metabotropic manner (Dore et al., 2016) and facilitate spontaneous transmitter release independent of Ca2+ influx (Abrahamsson et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Abrahamsson et al., 2017).

claims.claim: The open channel blocker MK-801 robustly reduced short-term plasticity at mf synapses, supporting an ionotropic mechanism that involves Ca2+ influx through presynaptic NMDA receptors.
claims.source: Our findings demonstrating that the open channel blocker MK-801 robustly reduced short-term plasticity at mf synapses support an ionotropic mechanism that involves Ca2+ influx through preNMDARs.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by experimental data in Figures 1-4.

claims.claim: A previous study failed to observe Ca2+ reductions in mf boutons by DL-APV.
claims.source: A previous study failed to observe Ca2+ reductions in mf boutons by DL-APV (Liang et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Liang et al., 2002).

claims.claim: A combination of factors could account for the discrepancy between the current study and a previous study that failed to observe Ca2+ reductions in mf boutons by DL-APV.
claims.source: A combination of factors could account for this discrepancy with our study, including a stronger mf repetitive stimulation (20 pulses, 100 Hz), which may overcome a less potent NMDAR antagonism and/or the need for preNMDAR activity, as well as the use of a higher affinity Ca2+ indicator (Fura-2 AM) and a lower spatiotemporal resolution imaging approach.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion as an explanation for discrepant findings.

claims.claim: Presynaptic NMDAR activation by either repetitive activation of mfs or two-photon glutamate uncaging increases presynaptic Ca2+.
claims.source: Nevertheless, in line with previous studies that detected presynaptic Ca2+ rises following local activation of NMDARs (e.g. NMDA or glutamate uncaging) in visual cortex (Buchanan et al., 2012) and cerebellum (Rossi et al., 2012), we provide direct evidence that preNMDAR activation by either repetitive activation of mfs or 2PU of glutamate increases presynaptic Ca2+ (Figures 5 and 6).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by calcium imaging data in Figures 5 and 6.

claims.claim: The Ca2+ targets of presynaptic NMDA receptors remain unidentified but may include proteins of the release machinery, calcium-dependent protein kinases and phosphatases, and Ca2+ release from internal stores.
claims.source: Although the Ca2+ targets remain unidentified, these may include proteins of the release machinery, calcium-dependent protein kinases and phosphatases, and Ca2+ release from internal stores (Banerjee et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation to previous work (Banerjee et al., 2016).

claims.claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors can promote spontaneous neurotransmitter release as indicated by changes in miniature, action potential-independent activity.
claims.source: In addition to facilitating evoked neurotransmitter release, preNMDARs can promote spontaneous neurotransmitter release as indicated by changes in miniature, action potential-independent activity (e.g. mEPSCs) (for recent reviews, see Banerjee et al., 2016; Kunz et al., 2013; Wong et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous reviews (Banerjee et al., 2016; Kunz et al., 2013; Wong et al., 2021).

claims.claim: A potential role for presynaptic NMDA receptors in spontaneous, action potential-independent release at mf synapses cannot be discarded.
claims.source: A potential role for preNMDARs in spontaneous, action potential-independent release at mf synapses cannot be discarded.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion as a speculative possibility.

claims.claim: Activation of presynaptic NMDA receptors by physiologically relevant patterns of presynaptic activity enhanced mf transmission and DG-CA3 information transfer.
claims.source: Our results show that activation of preNMDARs by physiologically relevant patterns of presynaptic activity enhanced mf transmission and DG-CA3 information transfer (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by data in Figure 4.

claims.claim: NMDAR genetic deletion in GCs resulted in memory deficits (e.g. pattern separation).
claims.source: A previous study reported that NMDAR genetic deletion in GCs resulted in memory deficits (e.g. pattern separation) (McHugh et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (McHugh et al., 2007).

claims.source: Although the mechanism is unclear, it could involve activity-dependent preNMDAR regulation of mf excitatory connections.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion as a speculative mechanism.

claims.claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptor specificity strongly suggests that these receptors have distinct roles in controlling information flow in cortical microcircuits.
claims.source: Like in neocortex (Larsen and Sjöström, 2015), such specificity strongly suggests that preNMDARs have distinct roles in controlling information flow in cortical microcircuits.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation to previous work (Larsen and Sjöström, 2015).

claims.claim: Presynaptic NMDA receptors have been implicated in the induction of LTP and LTD at excitatory or inhibitory synapses in several brain areas.
claims.source: PreNMDARs have been implicated in the induction of LTP and LTD at excitatory or inhibitory synapses in several brain areas (Banerjee et al., 2016; Wong et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous reviews (Banerjee et al., 2016; Wong et al., 2021).

claims.claim: Long-term forms of presynaptic plasticity at mf synapses can occur in the absence of NMDAR activation using robust induction protocols in vitro.
claims.source: While most evidence, at least using robust induction protocols in vitro, indicates that long-term forms of presynaptic plasticity at mf synapses can occur in the absence of NMDAR activation (Castillo, 2012; Nicoll and Schmitz, 2005), our findings do not discard the possibility that preNMDARs could play a role in vivo during subtle presynaptic activities.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Castillo, 2012; Nicoll and Schmitz, 2005).

claims.claim: BDNF-TrkB signaling is implicated in mf-CA3 LTP.
claims.source: As previously reported for corticostriatal LTP (Park et al., 2014), preNMDARs could regulate long-term synaptic plasticity by controlling BDNF release, which is consistent with BDNF-TrkB signaling being implicated in mf-CA3 LTP (Schildt et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Schildt et al., 2013).

claims.claim: In vivo evidence for the involvement of presynaptic NMDA receptors in brain function and disease is rather indirect.
claims.source: At present, however, in vivo evidence for the involvement of preNMDARs in brain function and disease is rather indirect (Bouvier et al., 2015; Wong et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations to previous work (Bouvier et al., 2015; Wong et al., 2021).

results.result: Electron microscopy with immunogold labeling revealed presynaptic NMDA receptors (GluN1 subunit) at mossy fiber terminals. GluN1 localized to ~32% of presynaptic particles at mf synapses compared to <10% at associational-commissural synapses, while AMPA receptors showed only ~5% presynaptic localization at both synapse types.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 provide converging anatomical evidence from electron microscopy with quantitative immunogold particle distribution analysis (Figure 1A-D and supplement 1). The differential localization between mf and ac synapses, and the control showing minimal AMPAR presynaptic localization, strengthen the specificity of the finding. Sample size (n=3 animals) is modest but appropriate for EM studies.

results.result: Pharmacological blockade of NMDARs with MK-801, D-APV, or R-CPP significantly reduced low-frequency facilitation (LFF) of both AMPAR-EPSCs and KAR-EPSCs at mossy fiber-CA3 synapses. Control experiments showed stable LFF in naïve slices and confirmed that intracellular and bath-applied MK-801 produced equivalent NMDAR blockade.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C10 demonstrate robust pharmacological evidence with multiple NMDAR antagonists, appropriate statistical tests (paired t-tests, Wilcoxon tests), and critical controls including stability experiments and verification of postsynaptic NMDAR blockade (Figure 1E-G and supplements 2-3). The use of both AMPAR and KAR recordings under different network excitability conditions strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: Genetic deletion of Grin1 from dentate granule cells using AAV5-CaMKII-Cre-GFP in Grin1 floxed mice eliminated NMDAR-EPSCs in granule cells without affecting basal transmitter release (paired-pulse ratio).
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C12, C15 establish the genetic deletion approach with appropriate controls (Figure 2A-C). The verification of NMDAR deletion via NMDAR/AMPAR ratio measurements and the lack of effect on paired-pulse ratio provide strong validation. However, the claim about LFF reduction (implied but not explicitly listed here) would complete this result.

results.result: NMDAR antagonism reduced LFF in transected mossy fiber axons and with focal D-APV application in stratum lucidum, demonstrating that the effect is independent of somatodendritic NMDARs in granule cells. Control experiments confirmed the spatial specificity of D-APV puff application.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C21 address a critical alternative explanation through axon transection experiments and focal drug application (Figure 3 and supplement 1). The controls showing D-APV blocks NMDARs in CA3 but not in distant DG, and stability in ACSF puff conditions, provide strong evidence that the effect is presynaptic. The experimental design effectively rules out somatodendritic contributions.

results.result: Presynaptic NMDARs enhance burst-induced facilitation at mossy fiber synapses during physiologically relevant activity patterns (5 pulses at 25 Hz). Both genetic deletion (Grin1-cKO) and pharmacological blockade (MK-801) reduced facilitation and decreased action potential firing in CA3 pyramidal neurons, demonstrating functional impact on information transfer.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C31 demonstrate the physiological relevance of preNMDARs using burst stimulation protocols that mimic in vivo granule cell firing (Figure 4 and supplements 1-3). The convergence of optogenetic, pharmacological, and electrophysiological approaches, along with both voltage-clamp and current-clamp recordings, provides robust evidence. Controls show stability and verify postsynaptic NMDAR blockade during burst stimulation.

results.result: Presynaptic NMDARs contribute to presynaptic calcium rise in mossy fiber boutons. Calcium transients elicited by action potential bursts were significantly reduced in Grin1-cKO animals compared to controls, and D-APV reduced the fifth peak of calcium transients under physiological Mg2+ conditions without affecting the first peak.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C36 provide direct evidence for the mechanism using two-photon calcium imaging (Figure 5 and supplement 1). The genetic and pharmacological approaches converge, and the selective effect on later peaks during burst activity (P5 but not P1) is consistent with activity-dependent NMDAR activation. The use of physiological Mg2+ concentrations strengthens the relevance. Sample sizes are adequate for imaging studies.

results.result: Two-photon glutamate uncaging experiments demonstrated that burst stimulation (5 pulses at 25 Hz), but not single pulses, induces calcium transients in mossy fiber boutons through activation of presynaptic NMDARs. These calcium transients were abolished by D-APV and were absent in Grin1-cKO animals, independent of laser power intensity.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C44 provide elegant mechanistic evidence using glutamate uncaging to directly activate preNMDARs (Figure 6 and supplements 1-3). The laser power control experiments (C38, C42) rule out technical artifacts. The requirement for burst vs. single pulse stimulation (C39, C43) demonstrates activity-dependence. The convergence of genetic deletion, pharmacological blockade, and the specificity for boutons vs. dendritic spines strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: GluN1-deficient mossy fiber boutons showed approximately 50% impairment in BDNF release compared to controls during both repetitive stimulation (125 pulses at 25 Hz) and burst stimulation (5 pulses at 100 Hz), as measured by BDNF-pHluorin imaging.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C48 demonstrate a functional consequence of preNMDAR activation using BDNF-pHluorin imaging (Figure 7 and supplement 1). The effect is observed with two different stimulation protocols, strengthening the conclusion. Statistical significance is achieved with appropriate sample sizes (9-11 slices per group). The ~50% reduction is substantial and biologically meaningful.

results.result: PreNMDAR modulation of mossy fiber transmission is target cell-specific: MK-801 had no effect on burst-induced facilitation or depression at mf-CA3 interneuron synapses but reduced low-frequency facilitation at mf-mossy cell synapses, similar to mf-CA3 pyramidal neuron synapses.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C52 demonstrate target cell specificity through recordings from different postsynaptic cell types (Figure 8 and supplement 1). The lack of effect on interneurons (C49) with appropriate controls (C51) contrasts with the effect on mossy cells (C50) and pyramidal neurons. This specificity is important for understanding circuit function, though the mechanism underlying this specificity is not addressed.

results.result: The study demonstrates that presynaptic NMDA receptors at mossy fiber boutons can be activated by physiologically relevant activity patterns and selectively enhance short-term synaptic plasticity at excitatory but not inhibitory synapses. PreNMDARs facilitate BDNF release, contribute to presynaptic calcium rise, and thereby fine-tune mossy fiber neurotransmission to control information transfer during dentate granule cell burst activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C58 represent the main conclusions synthesized from the experimental results. These summary claims are well-supported by the convergence of anatomical (C1-C4), pharmacological (C5-C10), genetic (C11-C12), electrophysiological (C16-C31), calcium imaging (C32-C44), BDNF release (C45-C48), and target specificity (C49-C52) evidence. The mechanistic link through calcium is directly demonstrated.

results.result: The Introduction contextualizes the study by citing prior work on presynaptic NMDARs in other brain regions, the unique properties of mossy fiber-CA3 synapses including robust frequency facilitation, and the high BDNF expression in mossy fibers with prior evidence for preNMDAR involvement in BDNF release at corticostriatal synapses.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C67 accurately represent prior literature based on the citations provided. These claims establish the scientific context and rationale for the study. The citations appear appropriate for the statements made, though verification of the cited work's actual findings would require examining the original papers.

results.result: The Discussion interprets the findings in context, noting that preNMDARs at mf-CA3 synapses are adjacent to release sites (suggesting direct control), facilitate transmission in a target-specific manner that may fine-tune excitatory/inhibitory balance, and could provide a site for neuromodulatory control and potential involvement in long-term plasticity through BDNF release.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C77 represent interpretations and speculations based on the experimental findings. C69 is supported by the EM data (C1-C4). C71-C72 are supported by the target specificity data (C49-C52). C73-C77 are reasonable speculations based on the findings and prior literature, appropriately qualified with terms like 'may' and 'could.' These interpretive claims are consistent with the data presented.

results.result: The Discussion notes the broader implications: NMDAR dysregulation is implicated in brain disorders, preNMDAR expression/function may be altered in disease models, specific preNMDAR tools are needed for in vivo studies, and dentate granule cells fire in brief bursts in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C81 cite relevant prior literature to contextualize the potential significance of the findings. C78-C79 are supported by the cited references. C80 is a reasonable statement about future research needs. C81 establishes the physiological relevance of the burst stimulation protocols used, supported by multiple citations to in vivo recording studies.

results.result: The Discussion addresses methodological considerations, noting that immunogold EM is more precise than immunoperoxidase EM, that preNMDARs are well-positioned near active zones, and that prior work suggested somatodendritic NMDARs could signal to terminals, but the current experiments with focal antagonism and axon transection make this explanation extremely unlikely.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C98 address important methodological and interpretive issues. C94 is a general statement about EM methods supported by citations. C95 is supported by the EM data (C1-C4). C96-C97 cite prior work raising alternative explanations. C98 is strongly supported by the experiments in Figure 3 (C16-C21) that directly test and rule out the somatodendritic explanation.

results.result: The Discussion addresses the mechanism of preNMDAR activation, noting that while preNMDARs can act as coincidence detectors at some synapses, this may not be essential at mf synapses given that NMDAR conductance is non-zero at rest, mf preNMDARs may exhibit low voltage dependence, and excitatory presynaptic potentials in granule cells might alleviate magnesium blockade.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C105 discuss the mechanism of preNMDAR activation with a mix of established facts (C102 supported by citations) and speculations (C101, C103, C105). C100 is supported by the LFF data (C5-C10). The speculative claims (C101, C103, C105) are reasonable given the data but lack direct experimental support in this study. The discussion appropriately qualifies these as possibilities ('may,' 'might,' 'conceivable').

results.result: The Discussion addresses developmental aspects, noting that preNMDARs are downregulated during development in neocortex and hippocampus, but functional preNMDARs were detected in young adult animals in this study. PreNMDARs have been identified in axonal growth cones and could play roles in immature mf synapses and adult neurogenesis, and experience can modulate preNMDAR expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C110 discuss developmental considerations. C106 is supported by citations to prior work. C107 is supported by the experimental data throughout the manuscript using P17-P28 rats and P30-P44 mice. C108 is supported by citations. C109-C110 are reasonable speculations based on cited literature, appropriately qualified. The age range used in the study is clearly stated in the methods.

results.result: The Discussion addresses the source of glutamate activating preNMDARs, noting it could come from multiple sources, but the results indicate activity-dependent release likely from mf boutons. At other synapses (medial entorhinal-GC), preNMDARs are localized away from release sites facing astrocytes, consistent with gliotransmitter activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C113 discuss the glutamate source for preNMDAR activation. C111 is a general statement about possibilities. C112 is supported by the activity-dependence shown in the burst stimulation and glutamate uncaging experiments (C39-C44). C113 cites prior work showing different preNMDAR localization at other synapses, providing useful context for the mf findings (C69).

results.result: The Discussion addresses the mechanism of preNMDAR-mediated facilitation, noting it may involve Ca2+ influx and/or depolarization activating voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, supported by NMDAR Ca2+ permeability and common mechanisms at other synapses. While metabotropic actions are possible, the MK-801 data support an ionotropic mechanism. The findings are consistent with prior studies showing presynaptic Ca2+ rises from NMDAR activation, despite one discrepant study that may be explained by methodological differences.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C124 discuss mechanisms with appropriate citations. C114-C117 cite relevant prior work on mechanisms. C118-C119 acknowledge alternative possibilities. C120 is strongly supported by the MK-801 data (C5-C7, C16, C23, C27). C121-C122 address a discrepant prior study with reasonable explanations for the difference. C123 is supported by the calcium imaging data (C32-C44). C124 is appropriately speculative about downstream targets.

results.result: The Discussion notes that preNMDARs can promote spontaneous neurotransmitter release at some synapses (a possibility not ruled out at mf synapses), that preNMDAR activation by physiological activity patterns enhanced mf transmission and information transfer, and that prior NMDAR deletion in GCs caused memory deficits that could involve preNMDAR regulation of mf connections.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C129 discuss additional functional implications. C125 cites prior reviews on spontaneous release. C126 appropriately notes this wasn't tested. C127 is strongly supported by the burst stimulation data (C22-C31). C128 cites prior work on memory deficits. C129 is reasonable speculation connecting the prior behavioral findings to the current mechanistic results.

results.result: The Discussion addresses implications for plasticity, noting that preNMDAR specificity suggests distinct roles in circuit control, that preNMDARs have been implicated in LTP/LTD at various synapses, that mf LTP can occur without NMDAR activation in vitro but preNMDARs could play roles in vivo, and that BDNF-TrkB signaling is implicated in mf-CA3 LTP. Current in vivo evidence for preNMDAR involvement in brain function is indirect.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C134 discuss plasticity implications. C130 is supported by the target specificity data (C49-C52) and cites similar findings in neocortex. C131-C133 cite relevant prior literature. C132 appropriately qualifies that the current findings don't contradict prior work on NMDAR-independent mf LTP. C134 accurately notes the limitation of current in vivo evidence, supporting the call for better tools (C80).
